title: Like all the nations (1 Samuel 8)
hook: the people ask for a king like everyone else, and Samuel warns them

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mother naming her son Ichabod on the day the ark was taken. Your line was the glory departed. Did you let someone name a loss without hurrying them? Today, years later, the people want something new. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

Samuel is old now. He has judged Israel for a lifetime, going round a circuit from town to town, and he has made his sons judges after him. It doesn't work. His sons, the text says, did not walk in his ways. They turned aside after gain, took bribes, and bent justice. So the elders of Israel gather and come to Samuel at his home in Ramah, and they put it plainly. You are old. Your sons don't walk in your ways. And then the request: now make us a king to judge us, like all the nations.
screen: `SAMUEL IS OLD.` → `HIS SONS TAKE BRIBES.` → `MAKE US A KING.`

segments.voice: Notice that their complaint is fair. Samuel's sons really are corrupt. The text says so before the elders do. But listen to the last phrase. Not just, give us a better judge. Like all the nations. They want to look like everyone around them. The thing displeases Samuel, and he prays. And the answer he gets is surprising. Listen to the people, God tells him: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me, that I should not be king over them. And still, give them what they ask. But warn them first. So Samuel tells them what a king will do. He will take your sons for his chariots and his horsemen, to run before his chariots, to plow his ground and reap his harvest and make his weapons. He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks and bakers. He'll take your best fields and vineyards and give them to his servants, and a tenth of your grain and your flocks. Listen to the verb. Take, and take, and take. And you, he says, will be his servants, and you'll cry out on that day because of the king you chose. Then the people answer, and they could not be plainer. No; but we will have a king over us; that we also may be like all the nations, that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles. They've heard the cost, and they still want it: a king to judge them and fight their battles, and to be like everyone else. God tells Samuel: listen to their voice, and make them a king. Some readers hear in this chapter a warning about power. Others hear something closer: how badly people can want to be like everyone else.
screen: `A FAIR COMPLAINT: CORRUPT SONS.` · `THEY REJECTED ME, NOT YOU.` · `TAKE, AND TAKE, AND TAKE.` · `WE WILL HAVE A KING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `THAT WE ALSO MAY BE LIKE ALL THE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask why you want what others have. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting lately: a phone, a look, a car, a job title, a kind of vacation, a kind of life. Hold it for a moment. Then ask Samuel's question, gently. What will it take from me? Time, money, attention, freedom? And ask the elders' question, honestly: do I want it because it's good, or because everyone around me has one? You don't have to decide anything. Just see the reason clearly. The bell holds the time.
Like all the nations. What the elders of Israel ask Samuel for: a king, so that they can be like everyone around them, even after he tells them what a king will take. Today's word.
Your line: like all the nations. Today, the next time you reach for something because everyone has one, pause and ask what it will take from you. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish commentators differ on this chapter: some read the request for a king as wrong in itself, others read Deuteronomy as allowing a king and fault only the people's motive, to be like the nations.

original.note: Hebrew: like all the nations, the elders' phrase in 1 Samuel 8:5 and 8:20.

trapdoor: what you thought: the people just wanted a better leader.
what it means: they wanted to be like everyone else, heard what it would cost, and asked anyway.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 17 already imagines Israel saying it wants a king like the nations, and sets limits on him.

notes: Audit: 'riding' (not in 7:16) changed to 'going round'; the narrator's 'because everyone else has one' replaced with the reasons the people themselves give in 8:20 (judge us, go out before us, fight our battles), so the elders are not reduced to envy.

All of 1 Samuel 8 is paraphrased close to the text without quotation marks (the JPS 1917 wording was not certain enough to quote). The screen line 'that we also may be like all the nations' follows 8:20 in the KJV.
'Riding a circuit from town to town' draws on 7:16; no count of towns is given.
